The Forward: Polish Investigators Tie Partisans to Massacre
The Jewish Chronicle: Bielski's son attacks Polish massacre 'lies'
Outono (Counting Stars): Naliboki: the savage murder of 128 Polish men, women and children by the Soviets

content.p: Before dawn on 8 May 1943, armed men entered Naliboki, a timber-built town of roughly three thousand people on the edge of a great forest in what had been eastern Poland and was by then under German occupation. By the time they left, 128 residents were dead, according to Poland's Institute of National Remembrance (IPN), the state body that investigates wartime crimes against Poles. The IPN's finding is that the attackers were Soviet partisans from units stationed in the Naliboki forest. No one was ever punished for the killings, Rzeczpospolita reports.

The massacre has had two lives. The first was local: a wartime atrocity in a region where Germans, Soviet partisans, the Polish underground and Jewish refugee fighters all competed for food and territory. The second began decades later, when a handful of witnesses and writers claimed that Jewish partisans under Tuvia Bielski had taken part, and the claim collided with a Hollywood film about the Bielski group. The IPN's own position on that claim is narrow, and it is worth stating exactly: it has not been proved.

Rzeczpospolita, in a 2007 long read, described Naliboki as a mostly wooden borderland town with a church, a synagogue and a few brick official buildings. By its account there were about three thousand inhabitants, including several hundred Jews. Soviet forces entered in September 1939; the Germans arrived in 1941, after which many of the town's Jews fled into the forest. A Jewish partisan unit led by Tuvia Bielski, a former Polish army corporal, began to form there around the turn of 1941 and 1942 with three of his brothers, and grew from about 40 people to several hundred, mostly women and children fleeing ghettos, the newspaper reported.

A blog account of the period describes a three-sided war. A unit of the Home Army, the main Polish resistance force loyal to the government in exile, operated in the forests and was largely cut off from other Polish units. According to that account, Soviet partisans repeatedly looted local farmers, talks between the Poles and the Soviets did not end the looting, and the residents formed a self-defence group. The Soviets demanded that the group submit to their command and the Poles refused; the blog says both sides then agreed not to attack each other. Rzeczpospolita quotes a survivor, Wacław Chilicki, saying the self-defence force was well armed, with dozens of rifles, several light machine guns, two heavy machine guns and a mortar, and that the Soviets wanted the weapons as well as revenge for the refusal. The newspaper also notes that the self-defence unit doubled as cover for the local Home Army detachment.

These accounts all come from the Polish side or from writers sympathetic to it. Rzeczpospolita itself sets beside them a Jewish version, in which Polish antisemites provoked the conflict by attacking Jews who left the ghettos for the forest. It quotes a memoir by Sulia Wolozhinska Rubin, whose husband took part in the Naliboki attack, that villagers rang bells and beat pots to warn others of passing Jews and partisans and then killed them with farm tools. Polish witnesses quoted in the same article dismissed her memoir as nonsense. The two versions are not reconciled by any court.

The IPN says the attack came in the early hours of 8 May 1943. Rzeczpospolita gives the most detailed eyewitness picture. Wacław Nowicki, then 18, recalled waking between half past four and five to a long burst of machine-gun fire through the walls of his family's house on the outskirts. The family barricaded themselves in and the attackers ran on towards the centre; he believes that saved them. Armed men, about 120 to 150 of them in the newspaper's telling, went from house to house. Chilicki, by then 83, said they killed everyone they met.

The newspaper reports that 128 or 129 people were killed, chiefly men and adolescent boys, but also a ten-year-old child and several women, one of whom died defending her three sons. In some families seven or eight members were killed. Some victims died in their beds; others were taken into yards and shot in groups. The church tower, the post office and the fire station were burned, and food, horses and cattle were stolen. Nowicki, who saw the aftermath, remembered burned buildings, piles of bodies and gunshot wounds. A different witness, Bolesław Chmara, then 15, described his older brother being called out onto the porch and shot.

The blog account adds that the Soviets burned the school as well, and it describes the killings as a "pacification". It says the commander of the "Stalin" brigade later reported to the NKVD that 250 residents had been killed and that 100 cows and 78 horses had been taken. It also says the commander claimed to have destroyed a German garrison in Naliboki, although there was no German garrison there. Rzeczpospolita makes a similar point, quoting the IPN historian Piotr Gontarczyk: a Soviet report of 10 May 1943 presented the massacre as the defeat of a strong German garrison.

The IPN's Łódź commission is investigating Soviet partisan crimes in the former Nowogródek province between 1942 and 1944, and Naliboki is one thread of that inquiry. Its public statement says the killers were Soviet partisans from units stationed in the Naliboki forest. It rests that on a report by Sidoruk, a secretary of the Lida underground district committee of the Belarusian Communist Party, sent to the central partisan headquarters in Moscow, which says the "Stalin" brigade carried out the attack. A 10 May 1943 order from "Platon", commander of the Baranowicze partisan grouping, confirms this and adds the "Dzerzhinsky", "Bolshevik" and "Suvorov" units.

The eyewitnesses questioned were less precise about the perpetrators. According to the IPN statement, their accounts of the attack and of the victims were detailed, but on who carried it out they were laconic: "bandits", "Soviet partisans", Jews, including former Naliboki residents. Rzeczpospolita reported that survivors had no doubt that a large part of the force came from the Bielski unit. Nowicki said that Jews who had lived among them before the war were prominent among the attackers and knew who lived where.

The prosecutor leading the case, Anna Gałkiewicz, told the newspaper in 2007 that investigators had examined all available documents, questioned about 70 witnesses and reconstructed the course of events as far as possible. She expected the case to close within a year or so, and the newspaper expected it to be discontinued because most perpetrators were probably dead. In January 2009 the IPN spokesman, Andrzej Arseniuk, still described the investigation as ongoing. This account does not record any later outcome.

The IPN's statement treats the Bielski allegation with care. Several witnesses briefly said that men "from Bielski" were among the attackers, but did not say on what basis, and no archival document supports them. Some historians also place the Bielski unit at the scene, the IPN says, but they do not cite sources for it. The statement also points to a memoir by a former Soviet partisan, published in the 1960s, which says Jewish family camps were set up in the Naliboki forest only in the second half of 1943, after the attack. The conclusion: the participation of Bielski partisans "is merely one of the versions of the investigated case."

The allegation has a traceable history. Gazeta Wyborcza noted in January 2009, as relayed by the Polish news agency, that Wacław Nowicki, a former resident, was the first to blame the Bielski brothers in his 1993 book "Żywe echa". Polish and Belarusian historians repeated the claim, among them Zygmunt Boradyn. In 2001 the Canadian Polish Congress pushed the IPN to open an investigation into partisans of what it called the Bielski brigade, the newspaper wrote.

The dispute reached the public in 2008 as the film Defiance, directed by Edward Zwick and starring Daniel Craig as Tuvia Bielski, neared release, based on a book by the historian Nechama Tec. Gazeta Wyborcza ran an article asking whether the film was about heroes or murderers. The Forward reported that Tec called the allegations "total lies" and that they "underline the antisemitic tendencies of the writers and the distortion of history". Tuvia Bielski's son Robert, quoted by The Jewish Chronicle, said the group did not reach the area until August 1943 and was about 50 kilometres away in May; the Forward's report likewise attributed to historians the belief that the partisans arrived only in August. Jack Kagan, a survivor of the Bielski group, called the accusation "a fabricated lie", while adding that he was not saying Jews did not take part in killings elsewhere.

Piotr Głuchowski, a Gazeta Wyborcza reporter who co-wrote the article, told the Forward he was sure the Bielski partisans were not involved, though he said the IPN was a serious organisation. He also told the Forward that the IPN was then dominated by members of the right-wing party Prawo i Sprawiedliwosc, a characterisation the IPN did not address; it declined to comment, citing the ongoing investigation.

Rzeczpospolita in 2007 showed how far apart the historians stand. It quotes Marek Chodakiewicz, a Washington-based historian, arguing that judgements of Bielski usually draw on sources from only one side, while Marian Turski, a historian and Polityka journalist, said partisans of every army took food from villagers. Israel Gutman of Yad Vashem was quoted as saying that the central fact was that Bielski saved about 1,200 people. The newspaper summed up the split: for some the legacy of Bielski is 1,200 saved, for others 130 murdered.

Rzeczpospolita reports that the perpetrators were never punished. A Polish defender, however, did stand trial. Eugeniusz Klimowicz, a Home Army officer and commander of the local self-defence, was accused by the communist authorities of murdering Soviet partisans, because defenders had shot several attackers on the night. He was sentenced to death in 1951, the sentence was commuted to life imprisonment, and the verdict was quashed in 1957.

Naliboki suffered again that summer. On 6 August 1943, German units conducting an anti-partisan operation codenamed "Hermann" entered the town, according to Rzeczpospolita, and the population was killed or sent to forced labour in the Reich, and the buildings that had survived the first attack were burned. The blog account says only that survivors were deported to Germany as labour. Tuvia Bielski, the paper adds, left for Palestine after the war, later lived in New York and died in 1987 aged 81.

The toll of 128 comes from the IPN. Rzeczpospolita says 128 or 129. The blog account says a Soviet commander reported 250 killed and that later investigation reduced the number to 128. The Forward's account of the IPN report gives the date as 8 March 1943, which conflicts with the IPN's own statement of 8 May. The size of the attacking force, about 120 to 150, rests on one newspaper article quoting the recollections of survivors.

What the opened pages establish is limited. A Soviet partisan attack killed 128 people in Naliboki, per the IPN. Soviet documents identify the brigades. Everything about Bielski participation remains a contested claim with no documentary proof, and the sources agree on little beyond that.
